The examples pin down every component except one: they fit two assignments that give opposite answers on all 16 inputs. So the answer is not determined; my predictions use one of them, which is a coin flip.

**Bit positions (Y)**
- **Y1 = bit 1.** In task X4-Y1-Z1, button 3 appears exactly when bit 1 is 1 in both stimuli. No other bit with any rule fits those three cases.
- **Y2 = bit 4**, from task X4-Y2-Z2.
- **Y3 = bit 2.** In task X6-Y3-Z4, every input giving 0 has bit 2 = 0 in both stimuli. In both Y3 tasks, the output depends only on whether the two bit-2 values match.

**Rule X4 = "both are 1"**, with:
- Z1: true → 3, false → 0
- Z2: true → 0, false → 1

**Two assignments fit all six known tasks:**

| | X6 | X2 | Z4 (true / false) | Z3 (true / false) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | at least one is 1 | exactly one is 1 | 2 / 0 | 3 / 2 |
| B | neither is 1 | both are the same | 0 / 2 | 2 / 3 |

Within each assignment, all X versions are distinct rules and all Z versions are distinct mappings. So nothing rules either one out.

**New task X2-Y1-Z1:** it looks at bit 1 of both stimuli.
- Under A, button 3 when the two bits differ and 0 when they match.
- Under B, the reverse: 3 when they match and 0 when they differ.

I went with A:

| # | Input | Bit 1 values | Prediction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0001 0001 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1110 0011 | 1, 0 | 3 |
| 3 | 1110 1000 | 1, 1 | 0 |
| 4 | 1011 0000 | 1, 0 | 3 |
| 5 | 1100 0000 | 1, 0 | 3 |
| 6 | 1000 1101 | 1, 1 | 0 |
| 7 | 0111 1101 | 0, 1 | 3 |
| 8 | 1001 0001 | 1, 0 | 3 |
| 9 | 0011 0111 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 0101 1100 | 0, 1 | 3 |
| 11 | 1000 1010 | 1, 1 | 0 |
| 12 | 0111 0110 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 13 | 1110 1101 | 1, 1 | 0 |
| 14 | 0110 0000 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 15 | 1111 1110 | 1, 1 | 0 |
| 16 | 0001 1101 | 0, 1 | 3 |

Under B, every prediction flips between 0 and 3. That puts my confidence at about 0.5.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
